question.prompt: If the six solutions of \(x^6=-64\) are written in the form \(a+bi,\) where \(a\) and \(b\) are real, then the product of those solutions with \(a\gt0\) is

solutions.explanation:
Factoring \(x^6+64\) will let us locate all six roots without needing an angle representation. First view it as a sum of cubes:
\[
x^6+64=(x^2+4)(x^4-4x^2+16).
\]
The remaining factor becomes a difference of squares after adding and subtracting the appropriate middle term:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^4-4x^2+16
&=(x^2+4)^2-(2\sqrt3\,x)^2\\
&=(x^2-2\sqrt3\,x+4)
  (x^2+2\sqrt3\,x+4).
\end{aligned}
\]
Completing the square in these two factors gives
\[
x^2-2\sqrt3\,x+4=(x-\sqrt3)^2+1,
\]
\[
x^2+2\sqrt3\,x+4=(x+\sqrt3)^2+1.
\]
Consequently the roots are
\[
\pm2i,\qquad \sqrt3\pm i,\qquad -\sqrt3\pm i.
\]
This list is exhaustive because every root must make one of the three quadratic factors zero, and each factor has exactly its two displayed roots.

Only \(\sqrt3+i\) and \(\sqrt3-i\) have positive real part; the roots \(\pm2i\) have real part zero and are excluded. The required product is
\[
(\sqrt3+i)(\sqrt3-i)=3-i^2=\boxed4,
\]
which is choice D.
solutions.title: Factor into simple quadratic equations

solutions.explanation:
Since the sixth power is the square of the cube, first observe that
\[
(x^3-8i)(x^3+8i)=x^6+64=0.
\]
Thus every solution satisfies \(x^3=8i\) or \(x^3=-8i\). In either case its cube has real part zero.

We only need solutions with positive real part, so write \(x=a+bi\), where \(a>0\) and \(b\) is real. Expanding with \(i^2=-1\) gives
\[
x^3=a(a^2-3b^2)+i\,b(3a^2-b^2).
\]
Its real part is zero, so
\[
a(a^2-3b^2)=0.
\]
Because \(a>0\), we may divide by \(a\), obtaining \(a^2=3b^2\). Substituting this into the imaginary part gives
\[
b(3a^2-b^2)=b(9b^2-b^2)=8b^3.
\]
The equation \(x^3=\pm8i\) therefore implies \(b^3=\pm1\). Since \(b\) is real, \(b=1\) or \(b=-1\). Then \(a^2=3\), and the condition \(a>0\) fixes \(a=\sqrt3\).

Both candidates \(\sqrt3\pm i\) do cube to \(\pm8i\), so both satisfy the original equation. The argument also shows that there are no other roots with positive real part. Their product is
\[
(\sqrt3+i)(\sqrt3-i)=3+1=\boxed4,
\]
which is choice D.
